records.name_note: NC State Extension's Common Name(s) list leads with "Seaoats" ("Sea Oats" second) and UF/IFAS FP594 heads its sheet "Uniola paniculata Sea Oats" with a Common name(s) value of "sea oats", but RHS's dedicated species page renders "North American spike grass" as the lead common name beneath the H1 "Uniola paniculata" and lists "sea oat" only under Other common names -- admissible sources split on which name is primary. Distinct from Chasmanthium latifolium, which this catalog already carries as Northern Sea Oats; Clemson HGIC's Ornamental Grasses factsheet says of that species, "This species is sometimes called northern sea oats."
unknowns: No admissible source scopes toxicity to cats or dogs specifically for Uniola paniculata; toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are left null rather than guessed.

is_houseplant is false: NC State, UF/IFAS FP594 and Clemson HGIC all describe this species exclusively as an outdoor native dune and landscape grass -- NC State gives it a Plant Type of Native Plant / Ornamental Grasses and Sedges, a USDA Plant Hardiness Zone range of 7a-11b and outdoor Landscape Location (Coastal), Landscape Theme (Drought Tolerant Garden, Native Garden) and Design Feature (Mass Planting) values, and UF/IFAS instructs "Place sea oats in an area of the landscape that receives full sun." No admissible source frames it as an indoor plant, so it lands false rather than null, per this catalog's landscape-plant rule.
No admissible source gives numeric day/night temperature ranges, humidity percentages, foot-candle light levels, or a chill-damage onset temperature for this species; those fields are left null.

direct_sun_hours_max is left null: NC State's '6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day' is the site-wide definition attached to its generic 'Full sun' light-category tag, not species-specific prose, per scope rules excluding NC State's light-category legend.

Legal protection/harvest status is captured here exactly as stated because the schema has no dedicated field for it: Clemson HGIC's Ornamental Grasses factsheet states 'Never collect or purchase wild collected plants, as they are protected by state law. Any person violating this law will be subject to fines and possible imprisonment.' HGIC's Salt Tolerant Plants for the South Carolina Coast factsheet separately lists sea oats as 'Protected by state law that prohibits picking or destroying the grass'. UF/IFAS (ask.ifas.ufl.edu/sg186) states 'Florida law prohibits the collection of sea oats inflorescences without a permit.' and, separately, 'It is illegal to collect sea oats for any reason in the wild without proper permitting.' UF/IFAS FP594 states 'It is illegal to collect plants from the wild without special permits.'

Salt tolerance is captured here exactly as stated because the schema has no dedicated field, and admissible sources use different scales: HGIC's Salt Tolerant Plants factsheet rates sea oats' salt tolerance as 'High salt tolerance'. UF/IFAS FP594's Culture table rates its 'Soil salt tolerances' as 'good'. UF/IFAS sg186 states 'This plant is extremely drought- and salt-tolerant, grows up to the high tide line of beaches.' NC State has no Tolerances field for this species; its Description prose says 'It tolerates dune conditions with blowing sand, drought and brief inundations of saltwater.'

Fertilizing: sources recommend against routine fertilizing rather than giving a strength or interval. HGIC states 'Do not fertilize sea oats.' UF/IFAS (ask.ifas.ufl.edu/sg186) states 'When growing sea oats, minimal fertilizer and irrigation inputs is encouraged.' fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, and fertilize_strength are left null accordingly rather than forced into the strength enum.

water_regime is left null: the watering-relevant statements found are UF/IFAS sg186's general low-input recommendation 'When growing sea oats, minimal fertilizer and irrigation inputs is encouraged.', HGIC's Salt Tolerant Plants factsheet's structured tag 'Water: dry', and UF/IFAS FP594's 'Drought tolerance: high'. None is a cadence, dry-down target, or day interval, and a structured water tag or drought-tolerance trait may not be read as one, so the field stays null for this in-ground perennial.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are left null: NC State's pH tolerance tags for Uniola paniculata span 'Acid (<6.0)', 'Neutral (6.0-8.0)', and 'Alkaline (>8.0)' -- both bounding bands are NC State's open-ended categories, which per the task rules must not be used to set a ceiling or floor -- and RHS's dedicated species page for Uniola paniculata does not publish a numeric soil pH field to check a ceiling against.

Missouri Botanical Garden / Plant Finder (plantfinder.mobot.org, www.missouribotanicalgarden.org) has no dedicated Plant Finder page for Uniola paniculata (only unrelated 'paniculata'-named species and a note that a different genus, Chasmanthium, was once called Uniola latifolia), so that admissible source could not be used for this species.
extension.psu.edu, extension.umd.edu, and fieldreport.caes.uga.edu did not turn up species-specific pages for Uniola paniculata and were not used.

RHS's dedicated species page for Uniola paniculata carries only taxonomic/administrative content: the binomial heading, the common name 'North American spike grass' (as the subtitle and inside an 'Other common names' value reading 'North American spike grass, sea oat, seaside oats'), a Botanical Details block (Family: Poaceae; Native to GB/Ireland: No; an empty Genus row; Name Status: Correct) and a Size module whose only row reads 'Time to Maturity: No preference'. It carries no cultivation, sun-exposure, hardiness-rating or soil fields, so several fields that might otherwise draw on RHS could not be supported from it.

Source-class note: Clemson HGIC's Ornamental Grasses and Grass-like Plants factsheet and its Salt Tolerant Plants for the South Carolina Coast factsheet are multi-species factsheets, not dedicated single-species pages. Their Sea Oats entries are used here only as corroboration for soil_drainage and for the protection-status and salt-tolerance disclosures above; every field value in this record rests on the dedicated single-species pages (NC State's Uniola paniculata page and UF/IFAS FP594).

records.name_note: UF/IFAS's dedicated single-species page (SG185) titles and H1s the species 'Seaside Goldenrod, Solidago sempervirens,' leading with 'Seaside Goldenrod.' NC State's dedicated page renders its H1 as the binomial alone and lists common names under a separate 'Common Name(s):' heading as three stacked, alphabetized, unranked entries — 'Goldenrod', 'Northern Seaside Goldenrod', 'Seaside Goldenrod'. Its first entry, 'Goldenrod', is a genus-level umbrella term (the same page notes the genus contains about 120 species), and 'Northern Seaside Goldenrod' is an additional common name for this same species, not a sibling species. common_name therefore follows the UF/IFAS title-led name.

NC State's description explicitly instructs 'Do not fertilize this goldenrod,' but gives no numeric interval, active months, or dilution strength, so fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, and fertilize_strength are left null rather than invented; this no-fertilize guidance is decision-relevant even though no schema field captures it directly.

The RHS species page (id 86726, Name Status: Correct) is a sparse profile — it carries only Family, Native to GB/Ireland, Genus (genus-level boilerplate), and Name Status, with no Sunlight/Position, Soil, Moisture, pH, Hardiness rating, or Cultivation paragraph for this species, unlike some of its cultivar pages. No RHS-sourced values were used for growing-condition fields as a result.

Salt tolerance is heavily and consistently documented by admissible sources but has no dedicated schema field: NC State tags this species '#salt tolerant' and lists 'Salt' under Resistance To Challenges, describing it in prose as 'highly salt tolerant'; UF/IFAS (SG185) states it is 'highly tolerant of both saline soils and salt spray.' Both are species-specific to Solidago sempervirens, not genus-level claims.

NC State's dedicated page explicitly attributes the hay-fever/ragweed confusion to goldenrods generally ('Goldenrods have been wrongfully accused of causing hay fever which is actually an allergic reaction to wind-borne pollen from ragweed') and separately notes 'The Seaside Goldenrod may get confused with one of its cousins' (other Solidago species, not ragweed) — this content was intentionally excluded from all schema fields since it is not evidence for any listed field.

is_houseplant is set to false on the basis that NC State's dedicated species page frames Solidago sempervirens entirely as an outdoor coastal/landscape border plant (Habitat: coastal dunes, dune slacks, maritime wet grasslands, tidal marshes; Landscape Location: Coastal, Pond, Riparian) with no admissible source describing indoor/houseplant use.

Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder (plantfinder.mobot.org / missouribotanicalgarden.org) does not appear to carry a dedicated profile page for Solidago sempervirens specifically (only other Solidago species and cultivars were found), so it was not used as a source for this record.

Clemson HGIC, Penn State Extension, University of Maryland Extension, and UGA CAES Field Report did not surface a dedicated single-species page for Solidago sempervirens (only genus-level goldenrod/ragweed factsheets or multi-species native-plant lists), so they were not used as sources for this record.

records.name_note: Admissible sources split on which binomial is currently correct. RHS's dedicated Spartina alterniflora page gives this species a Name Status of "Correct" under Spartina alterniflora and lists "Spartina alterniflora var. glabra" as a synonym — it does not mention Sporobolus. Clemson HGIC's Blue Carbon factsheet (a multi-species topic page, not a dedicated single-species page) says South Carolina's coastal tidal marshes "are dominated by the salt-tolerant plant Sporobolous alterniflorus (commonly referred to by the previous scientific name Spartina alterniflora)," i.e. it treats Sporobolus alterniflorus as current and Spartina alterniflora as the prior name (the misspelling "Sporobolous" is Clemson's own and is kept inside the quotation). Because the only dedicated single-species page among admissible sources (RHS) affirms Spartina alterniflora as correct, scientific_name_given/accepted follow RHS, but the Sporobolus alterniflorus synonymy is disclosed here exactly as Clemson states it. On the common name, RHS renders "smooth cord grass" both as the subtitle beneath its heading and as its sole Other common names entry, and that is the name landed, title-cased; Clemson's salt-marsh factsheet writes it as "Smooth cordgrass".
unknowns: Across the ten admissible domains, only RHS (rhs.org.uk) has a dedicated single-species page for Spartina alterniflora (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/161332/spartina-alterniflora/details). plants.ces.ncsu.edu has dedicated pages for sibling species (Spartina pectinata, Spartina bakeri) but none for Spartina alterniflora, and neither /plants/spartina-alterniflora/ nor /plants/sporobolus-alterniflorus/ resolves there. plantfinder.mobot.org / missouribotanicalgarden.org, hgic.clemson.edu, edis.ifas.ufl.edu, ask.ifas.ufl.edu, extension.psu.edu, extension.umd.edu, and fieldreport.caes.uga.edu returned no dedicated single-species page for this species either — only multi-species or topic-level factsheets (e.g. Clemson's Blue Carbon and Life Along the Salt Marsh pages, UF/IFAS's Salt Marsh Restoration and Living Shorelines publications) that mention Spartina alterniflora among other marsh species. Those multi-species pages were not used to source any species-specific horticultural field; Clemson's Blue Carbon page is used only for the naming disclosure in name_note and its Life Along the Salt Marsh page only for the common-name variant and for the outdoor-siting basis of is_houseplant.

That legal-status note has no corresponding schema field, so it is recorded here rather than dropped.

is_houseplant is false: no admissible source makes an explicit indoor/houseplant statement either way, and RHS's dedicated page carries no cultivation content beyond a legal restriction on planting the species outdoors in the wild. The value rests on Clemson HGIC's salt-marsh factsheet placing the species in the outdoor intertidal salt marsh, 'often dominated by a monoculture of Spartina alterniflora as this plant can withstand the dynamic conditions created by the tides.' An intertidal marsh grass with no houseplant framing lands false, as elsewhere in this catalog; the thinness of that support is disclosed here rather than hidden.

records.name_note: Admissible sources split on which common name leads. Missouri Botanical Garden's dedicated species page names it "eastern baccharis" as the rendered value of its structured Common Name field, and NC State's dedicated page stacks ten alphabetized Common Name(s) entries (Consumptionweed, Consumption-Weed, Coyote Bush, Eastern Baccharis, Groundsel, High-tide Bush, Saltbush, Salt Marsh Elder, Sea Myrtle, Silverling), of which "Eastern Baccharis" is the fourth. unknowns: toxic_to_pets left null: the only admissible toxicity evidence found is scoped to cattle/livestock or is unscoped as to animal. NC State's Insects, Diseases, and Other Plant Problems line reads 'No significant problems. Weak wood is easily broken. Toxic to cattle if eaten in large quantities.' and Missouri Botanical Garden states 'The leaves are toxic to livestock if ingested in large quantities'. NC State's Fruit Description separately states 'Seeds are shed in late fall or winter, but the seeds of the female plant (this plant is dioecious) are poisonous.' -- an unqualified poisonous-part statement with no animal scope at all. None of these names cats or dogs, so per the rule that non-cat/dog-scoped toxicity evidence cannot support toxic_to_pets, both toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are left null; the full evidence is recorded here so nothing safety-adjacent is dropped.

soil_ph left null: NC State's Soil pH field shows an open-ended acid band ('Acid (<6.0)') and a closed neutral band ('Neutral (6.0-8.0)'). No floor can be read off the open-ended acid band. The neutral band's closed top of 8.0 would normally be checked against RHS's pH field before being used as soil_ph_max, but this species' RHS page carries no Soil or pH field to cross-check against, so no ceiling was set either.

water_regime left null: the structured watering field found, Missouri Botanical Garden's Water field, reads 'Medium to wet' — a range, not a cadence, and a soil-moisture descriptor rather than a regime statement, so per rules it cannot by itself support keep_moist or any other regime token. water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_estimate_basis, fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, fertilize_strength, humidity_need/pct, light_fc_min/good, direct_sun_hours_max, day/night temperature fields, and chill_damage_f are all left null: no admissible source frames this in-ground shrub/tree's care in those terms (day-interval watering, container fertilizing schedule, footcandle light levels, indoor temperature ranges, or a numeric chill-damage onset temperature); NC State's hardiness zones (5a-9b) are a survival range, not a damage-onset figure.

part_shade was dropped from outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State's Light field lists 'Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)', but Missouri Botanical Garden's structured Sun field for this species reads only 'Full sun' and its Culture note specifies '...well-draining soils in full sun', and RHS's species page carries no structured sun/position field to corroborate against, so only full_sun is retained. NC State's own Description prose ('Plant in full sun to partial shade in a range of soil types, including infertile and wet sites') and its '#shade shrub' tag are the same single source, and its tag list is site-wide legend vocabulary rather than species-specific structured sun evidence.

European invasive status was not asserted in this record's fields per the admissible-source-only instruction, but is documented here: RHS states this plant 'is listed as an invasive non-native species in the UK' and 'is on the GB Non-Native Species Secretariat list of Species of Special Concern and the EU list of Invasive Alien Species of Union Concern (applies in NI)'; Missouri Botanical Garden similarly notes it 'was introduced in Europe and Australia as an ornamental in the late 1800s to early 1900s and is now considered invasive in some areas.'

soil_drainage is left null. NC State's Soil Drainage field for this species renders five tags -- Frequent Standing Water, Moist, Occasional Flooding, Occasionally Dry, Occasionally Wet -- and does NOT carry Good Drainage or Well Drained, so this catalog's Good Drainage + Moist route to moderate does not apply, and the set is dominated by standing-water and flooding tolerance. Missouri Botanical Garden pulls both ways in one sentence: its structured Water field reads 'Medium to wet' and its Tolerate field 'Clay Soil, Dry Soil, Wet Soil, Shallow-Rocky Soil', while its Culture sentence requires 'evenly moist to wet, sandy to loamy, well-draining soils'. moisture_retentive needs an explicit consistently-wet cultivation requirement, and MoBot's own sentence asks for well-draining soil while NC State's prose frames the species as tolerating 'a range of soil types, including infertile and wet sites' -- adaptability, not a drainage requirement. The two admissible sources cannot be reconciled onto one token, so the field is null rather than moderate (which the audit refuted as resting on a tag set that never contains the moderate-defining tag).

The only requirement-shaped prose from any admissible source points to the well-drained end -- Clemson: 'Plant it in a sunny to partly shady location in well-drained neutral to acidic soil.' -- but the catalog's fast token needs sharp/sandy drainage with no wet tolerance described, and NC State carries 'Occasional Flooding' and states 'Once established, it is both drought tolerant and flood resistant.' Eight native coastal dune and salt-marsh plants: Sea Oats, American Beachgrass, Seaside Goldenrod, Sea Ox-eye, Smooth Cord Grass, Eastern Baccharis, Dwarf Palmetto, Saw Palmetto. Naming decisions: the three RHS lower-case names land title-cased (Sea Ox-eye, Smooth Cord Grass), except Ammophila breviligulata, which lands as American Beachgrass rather than RHS's 'American marram' -- no admissible North American source has a dedicated single-species page for it at all (NC State 404s), so the North American name rests on two multi-species lists, Clemson HGIC's Salt Tolerant Plants factsheet ('American Beach Grass') and UMD Extension's native-plant list ('dunegrass, American beachgrass'), with RHS's name recorded in name_note rather than adopted. Sea Oats is distinct from Chasmanthium latifolium, already in this catalog as Northern Sea Oats, and that is stated in name_note. Baccharis halimifolia lost part_shade from outdoor_sun_exposure (NC State-only, excluded by MoBot's structured Sun field) and both it and Serenoa repens keep soil_drainage null: the audit refuted 'moderate' for each and confirmed no replacement token, Baccharis because its NC State tag set carries no Good Drainage tag while MoBot's Culture sentence requires well-draining soil, Serenoa because its tags are tolerance tags with no Moist value and its only requirement-shaped prose is Clemson's well-drained sentence against NC State's flood-resistance. Sea Oats' soil_base and soil_drainage were re-based off the dedicated pages (NC State's Landscape Theme, Soil Drainage and Soil Texture fields, UF/IFAS FP594's landscape-siting sentence); the two Clemson multi-species factsheet citations that had carried them are relabelled as corroboration, and the one whose quote did not bear on soil_base at all was dropped. Sea Oats' legal-protection and salt-tolerance statements stay verbatim in unknowns, as does the 'Do not fertilize sea oats.' instruction -- no fertilize field was set from it. Saw Palmetto's petiole-spine handling warning stays verbatim in unknowns in the sources' own words. is_houseplant was set false with citations on the seven records that carried null; for the three records whose only dedicated page (RHS) carries no cultivation content at all -- American Beachgrass, Sea Ox-eye, Smooth Cord Grass -- it rests on a Clemson HGIC multi-species factsheet labelled as such in the claim and disclosed in unknowns, the only admissible outdoor-siting evidence that exists for those three. Borrichia frutescens keeps scientific_name_accepted null: RHS's Name Status for it reads 'Unresolved', and unknowns says so rather than landing a placeholder.
